extracted.intended_audience: IP professionals, technical experts, SEP holders and implementers, and readers interested in telecommunications patents and standards
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory explanatory guide describing what standard essential patents (SEPs) are, how they are declared and licensed, and what FRAND commitments mean in the telecommunications standards context.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a standard essential patent (SEP)?
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent that protects a technology that is necessary, namely “essential” to a standard is termed a standard essential patent. The term “standard” referred to here indicates a standard derived from technical specifications for specific technologies, such as radio technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common consumer products must meet many standards and require the patented technology to do so; manufacturing standard-compliant goods without employing key technologies covered by one or more SEPs is impossible. SEPs are patents like any other but include additional declaration information when declared at SSOs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentiality — cannot design around SEPs
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, companies can provide alternative inventions to work around an existing non-SEP to avoid patent infringement; however, they can’t design around a SEP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essentiality is what distinguishes SEPs from non-SEPs and is the basis for licensing demand; essentiality is often contested in litigation and technical disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and standard-setting organizations (SSOs) roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards are typically set by Standard-Setting Organizations (SSOs), such as ETSI in Europe and ATIS in the United States. The standards for telecommunication technologies are formulated according to technical specifications developed and provided by 3GPP, a consortium of regional SSOs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 3GPP provides the technical specifications and SSOs such as ETSI formulate the standards; ETSI’s IPR database is relatively more active, public, and transparent in the telecommunications sector.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEP declaration at SSOs (minimum required information)
rubrics_metrics.description: To declare a SEP at, for example, the ETSI IPR database, a patent owner needs to submit a declaration. The minimum mandatory information needed includes the standard/specification number and the patent application or publication number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should fill out the rest of the declaration with all relevant information (project names, releases, versions, etc.). A declaration may consist of several SEPs and their family members. Declarations produce a declaration number for each declared SEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping declared SEPs to technical specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The technology declared SEPs cover should be able to be mapped to its declared technical standards or specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declared SEPs will have declaration numbers and, in databases, users can often view corresponding 3GPP specifications and release information by clicking patent details (example: Apple’s 5G active SEP declaration list).

rubrics_metrics.name: SEP implementers must license from SEP holders
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers of standard-compliant goods (SEP implementers) that use the technology covered by at least one SEP will need to license the SEP(s) from the SEP holders (or owners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parties negotiate conditions and fees; the outcome is formalized in a license agreement that should reflect FRAND terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND commitment (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry representatives unite under SSOs to generate technical standards. Then SEP holders commit to making their patented technology accessible under Fair, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory (FRAND) terms (also known as RAND) in exchange for an agreed royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FRAND terms are a method to ensure that SEP implementors are able to license and use standardized technology on fair grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND — Fair
rubrics_metrics.description: Fair: it is usually quite easy to recognize unfair licensing requirements, e.g., it would be considered unfair to demand concessions that are not part of the licensing deal from a licensee, or to tie the grant of the license to unrelated commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness is subjective and more difficult to define in absolute terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND — Reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable: also a subjective theory, a good benchmark for evaluating reasonableness would be to compare with general industry practice, especially when discussing licensing royalty rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonableness is often assessed by comparison to industry norms and comparable licensing arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND — Non-discriminatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-discriminatory: licensees that are in similar situations should always receive the same terms and rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different treatment occurs, there should be objective grounds for the difference in treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: ETSI IPR Policy — irrevocable undertaking timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The ETSI IPR Policy requests SEP holders to provide “an irrevocable undertaking in writing” stating that it will grant “irrevocable licenses on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (“FRAND”) terms and conditions…” within three months after submitting a declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural SSO policy requirement tied to declarations; however, compliance and interpretation may be disputed and does not equate to an external regulatory enforcement mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND commitments are contractual/SSO-based, not regulatory
rubrics_metrics.description: FRAND terms are not regulatory, although we often refer to them as FRAND “obligations.” This merely means that SSO members agree to abide by FRAND terms when they declare SEPs at such SSOs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no specific entity designated to enforce FRAND terms; disputes are typically resolved through litigation, courts, or antitrust processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispute resolution — litigation and antitrust
rubrics_metrics.description: When SEP holders and implementers cannot come to a licensing agreement, the dispute is usually brought to various courts around the world. We sometimes see SEP disputes in antitrust cases where a patent owner declines to grant a license or refuses to grant the license on FRAND terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts or juries may determine FRAND terms and royalty rates; SEP litigation has involved major industry players and can be protracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-declaration of SEPs (risk and causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard essential patents are typically self-declared by patent-holding businesses as essential for the implementation of standards. The declared SEPs are not subject to any kind of review to determine their supposed essentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and financial motivations can lead to over-declaration; determining essentiality is often contested and is a common source of SEP litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of standardized declaration data and completeness issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations are made to various regional SSOs and not to a single international entity, making it difficult to unify and compile declaration data. Only the patent/application number and technical specification/standard are mandatory in submitting a declaration to ETSI; many SEP declarations lack other relevant information such as version number, release information, or project names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incomplete or inconsistent data (including assignee versus actual owner/subsidiary discrepancies) makes SEP data work tedious and time-consuming for analysts and negotiators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty in determining royalty rates
rubrics_metrics.description: As FRAND is a subjective matter, disagreements over the royalty rates in SEP licensing agreements often arise and prolong negotiations. The essentiality of a SEP or SEPs must first be determined and followed by the exact royalty rate the licensee is willing to pay and the licensor is willing to accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiations can take several months to years; examples include long-running disputes such as Ericsson and Samsung’s 2014 licensing workups. Determining royalty rates often requires technical assessment of essentiality and benchmarking to industry practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards evolve and require version/release tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: The standards for each technology may undergo continuous improvement and revisions and are updated from time to time according to their relevant technical specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because standards change across releases, declarations and licensing analyses should track project names, releases, and version information to assess applicability and essentiality.
